masthead_title: Hot data meets cold trade winds
regime_line: Friday's blowout business survey (the strongest in 52 months) pushed the whole yield curve up — including, for the first time all week, short-term rates — and the weekend added new pressure: the U.S.–Canada tariff pause broke down and new Iran sanctions landed, with Nvidia earnings and the Fed's Jackson Hole gathering ahead. Long rates wear both watch-list flags this morning.
provenance_note: Stated reasons via web search with named-source attribution (the standing source): Yahoo Finance, CNBC, TheStreet, Benzinga, Motley Fool. This edition was generated manually — the 6:30am cloud run is blocked by a network-policy issue (see Flags).
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — the first final grade

  • CL-0001 — REFUTED. Wednesday morning we said: if the Fed minutes sounded hawkish, long rates would push past Monday's 5.31% high within two days. They never did — Thursday closed 5.23%, Friday 5.27%. The claim is graded refuted, with an honest asterisk the ledger now records permanently: the minutes did lean hawkish, but the Treasury simultaneously doubled its long-bond buybacks ($2B to at least $4B per operation, per Secretary Bessent — Yahoo Finance), which capped exactly the move the claim predicted. The prediction never conditioned on the government intervening in supply. Lesson banked: in this regime, the debt manager is a player, not a spectator — future long-end claims get written with that in mind.
  • CL-0002 (AI-chip selloff was rate-rotation, not demand doubt) — interim: tight. Chips lagged the market by another 0.81 points Friday; the running tally is −1.42 of the −2.0 that would refute it, with one day left (grades Wednesday morning on Tuesday's close). Worth noting either way: Nvidia reports this week — the real demand datapoint arrives just after this claim's deadline.
  • CL-0003 (long-rate rise is about the price of time, not inflation fear) — interim: holding by a single basis point. The 10-year breakeven — the market's implied inflation forecast — has crept up 10bp in a week to 2.34%, right against the claim's 2.35% line. Inflation expectations are starting to stir; if Tuesday's close crosses the line, the claim fails and that would be genuinely important information. Grades Wednesday.
  • CL-0004 (Walmart's miss signals broad consumer softness) — interim: moving toward refuted. Consumer-discretionary stocks outperformed the market by 0.74 points Friday — the opposite of what broad softness looks like. Day 1 of 5; due Friday.
story_html:
Friday's economic data was the hottest yet. S&P Global's flash composite PMI — an early monthly survey of business activity — jumped to 56.0, the strongest reading in 52 months, with the services side at 56.8 against expectations of 54.0 (Yahoo Finance/CNBC coverage). And this time the bond market's reaction had a new feature: it wasn't just long rates that rose. The 2-year Treasury — the rate that tracks what the Fed will actually do, which had sat frozen at 4.19% through the entire week's drama — moved up 5bp to 4.24%. In plain terms: after a week of arguing only about the price of lending long, the market started to also question whether the Fed stays this easy. The 10-year rose to 4.74% and the 30-year to 5.27%, and both carry watch-list flags this morning (higher than on all but a handful of days in the past six months). One note for the record: some Friday coverage quoted the 30-year "down around 5.23%" — that was intraday; the official close (treasury.gov) was 5.27%.

The weekend then changed the subject. The tariff pause with Canada that calmed markets on Wednesday broke down — talks failed, with reciprocal tariff threats now on the table — and the administration announced new economic sanctions on Iran (TheStreet, CNBC). Futures opened the week mixed-to-lower. As always here, tariffs are treated as mechanics, not politics: they are a cost that lands somewhere — in importers' margins, in consumer prices, or in exchange rates — and "which of those three" is the analytical question for the week. Oil is the other channel: WTI sits at 87.06, up 51.6% this year, and Iran sanctions press on exactly that.

Now the cross-asset check, because it's telling an interesting story: gold rose again Friday (+2.4% to 4,624) — its fifth straight weekly gain, the longest streak since last October (Benzinga) — and inflation breakevens have quietly climbed 10bp in a week. Gold rallying while yields rise is not the usual pattern; it reads like some investors buying insurance against inflation staying sticky even as growth runs hot. Credit remains completely calm (junk spreads at 2.73%, near the year's lows), and the equal-weight S&P is again unusually strong (+1.7σ) — the average stock keeps refusing to confirm any downturn story. This week supplies the two biggest tests in months: Nvidia's earnings (the AI demand question, answered with numbers) and Jackson Hole (the Fed's own voice, after a week when markets moved without it).
dashboard_lag_note: Observation dates in parentheses where they trail the 2026-08-21 market close: the TIPS real yield, breakeven, and both credit-spread series publish a day behind (§5); Fed balance sheet and TGA are weekly (08-19). Flagged rows (⚑): far outside the past-6-months normal range — see the Reading key below.
dashboard_interp_html: The shape of the move changed on Friday, and the table shows it: for the first time all week, everything rose together — 2Y +5bp, 10Y +5bp, 30Y +4bp — a parallel shift up rather than a long-end-only move. When the front end joins, the message shifts from "pay us more to hold long bonds" to "maybe the Fed itself stays tighter for longer." The 10Y and 30Y both wear flags (z +1.8 and +2.0), and the week's round trip is now complete: 30Y 5.31 → 5.19 → 5.27, ending 4bp below where the drama started — the buyback bought four basis points and four days, and hot data took the rest back. The quiet mover worth respect: the 10-year breakeven at 2.34% (+10bp on the week) — the market's inflation forecast waking up, and CL-0003's deadline is Tuesday. Plumbing is unchanged and unstressed: balance sheet $6.746T, the overnight cash buffer effectively empty, SOFR steady at 3.65% — this remains a bond-supply-and-data story, not a money-tightness story.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 502 S&P constituents scanned mechanically; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) — never by seeming interesting. 22 qualified Friday; cap is 3 names + a sector note. "Stated reason" is what reporting said, not necessarily what's true.

FCX +7.64% (76.66, from 71.22) — what happened: Freeport-McMoRan, the big copper miner, hit an all-time high. Stated reason: a broad rally in copper-linked stocks on tightening copper supply expectations and strong recent earnings, on a day of wide participation — 8 of 11 sectors up (Benzinga). Why it matters: copper is the metal the real economy is built from — wiring, construction, and increasingly datacenters. A copper miner at record highs alongside a 52-month-high business survey is the same message from two different markets: the industrial economy is running hot, which is exactly what keeps upward pressure on interest rates.

TSLA +5.14% (362.86, from 345.13) — what happened: the day's biggest mega-cap gain. Stated reason: approval to bring its robotaxis to Las Vegas, plus a confirmed European launch for its electric Semi truck (Motley Fool, Yahoo Finance). Why it matters: mostly company-specific — but it's a useful reminder that in a week when "AI hardware" sold off, the market kept paying up for AI applications with revenue attached. The selling has been about one tier of the AI trade, not the whole theme.

MRVL −5.57% (237.04, from 251.01) — what happened: down 5.6% two days after bouncing 5.8%. Stated reason: no company-specific catalyst surfaced in coverage — the chip complex stayed violently choppy (semis lost more than 4% on the week per CNBC). Why it matters: this whipsaw — down 8% Tuesday, up 6% Thursday, down 6% Friday — is what a market that has genuinely not made up its mind looks like. CL-0002 tracks the verdict, and Nvidia's earnings this week will out-vote everything that came before.

Sector note: Utilities fell 2.69 points behind the market (XLU −2.29% vs. SPY +0.41%) — the biggest sector gap of the day. Utilities are the stock market's closest cousin to a long bond: steady dividends, lots of debt, no growth story — so when long rates jump, they fall first and hardest. Friday they were the equity market agreeing with the Treasury market. Materials (+1.73 points ahead, led by the copper names) took the other side of the same trade: hot economy, higher rates, real assets bid.
chart_of_day_why: The 30-year Treasury yield still carries the morning's biggest watch-list flag (+2.0σ) and now tells the whole completed arc: Monday's 5.31% panic peak, Wednesday's 5.19% dip on the Treasury's buyback announcement, Friday's 5.27% close on blowout data. The buyback bought four basis points and four days; the data took the rest back — that tension is the backdrop for Jackson Hole this week.
tier3_html:
Daily read: chips lagged again Friday (SMH −0.40% vs. the market's +0.41%) and lost more than 4% on the week (CNBC) even as the index only slipped modestly — the group is still up 55.6% this year against the market's 12.3%. The whipsaw continues without a verdict. The verdict arrives this week: Nvidia reports earnings — the closest thing to a direct reading of real AI demand that markets get, and it lands two days after CL-0002's deadline. However that claim grades on Tuesday's close, Wednesday night's numbers matter more.

Financing watch: nothing new surfaced over the weekend on AI-adjacent issuance or structures; the standing items (Broadcom's XPV leasing vehicle; the Treasury buyback regime) stand as routed. Credit stayed indifferent through the week's equity chop — junk spreads at 2.73%, near the year's lows. The watch condition is unchanged: this section starts shouting when credit stops being calm, and it hasn't.
calendar_note_html: Today's slate is one speech: Treasury Secretary Bessent at 2pm — and given that his buyback expansion is the single biggest lever on the long end this month, it's the only 2pm speech this brief would call market-moving. The week's real weight comes later: Nvidia earnings and the Fed's Jackson Hole symposium, where Chair remarks traditionally reset the policy conversation — after a week in which markets repriced entirely without the Fed's voice.

concept_title: When the front end moves, the vote is about the Fed
concept_html: All week this space has leaned on one diagnostic: the 2-year Treasury didn't move, so the drama wasn't about the Fed. Friday that changed, and it's worth slowing down on why the 2-year is the tell. A 2-year note's return is dominated by the path of the Fed's overnight rate over the next 24 months — there's little room for anything else in it. So the 2-year is effectively a running poll of Fed expectations: when it jumps 5bp in a day, as it did Friday after a 52-month-high business survey, the market is saying "the odds of the Fed staying tighter for longer just went up." Long bonds carry that same expectation plus the extra compensation for time (the premium we covered in segment 2) — which is why a hot-data day moves the whole curve, while a supply announcement (Wednesday's buybacks) moves only the long end. Friday was the week's first genuine path repricing. It also reframes Jackson Hole: the market has already moved its Fed forecast; the Chair's speech now either validates that move or fights it — and either answer moves the 2-year first.
client_translation: "Watch the 2-year Treasury when big news hits: it's the market's live forecast of what the Fed does next. Last week it sat dead still through all the drama — until Friday's strong economic report nudged it up. That was the market quietly saying rate cuts just got a little less likely."
client_lens_html:
• "Are the tariffs back on?" — The Canada pause broke down over the weekend with reciprocal threats now in play. The useful frame for clients: a tariff is a cost that has to land somewhere — company margins, consumer prices, or currencies — and which one absorbs it determines whether it shows up in portfolios as an earnings problem or at the register as an inflation problem. Nobody knows the split yet; that's the honest answer.
  • "Why is gold at record levels if the economy is strong?" — Sharp question, because gold usually struggles when rates rise. Five straight weekly gains alongside rising yields and a +10bp creep in inflation expectations reads like insurance-buying against inflation staying sticky in a hot economy. Worth watching rather than explaining away — if breakevens keep climbing, the "inflation is settled" assumption gets tested (that's literally CL-0003, grading Wednesday).
  • "Should I be nervous about this week?" — It's a genuinely big one: Nvidia earnings (the AI demand question, answered with actual numbers) and Jackson Hole (the Fed's reply to a market that repriced without it). The portfolio answer isn't prediction — it's that weeks like this are why diversification across the things that disagreed last week (stocks, bonds, gold, energy) exists.
